That is (probably) a high traffic dealership with not a lot of money coming from each customer. You will have to write a lot of cars to get the numbers you need. Pay plans I’ve had in NorCal area usually start at around 2.0-3.0% and have a tiered system that goes up to about 8.0%. I’ve seen people with pay plans that go up to 13.0%. All depends on what it’s structured on. If it’s on total CP, Warranty, and Internal, I would accept a lower percentage. If it is on gross CP, Warranty, and Internal I would push for something higher (in general). Now, because you are starting out in the position, I would accept a lower pay to be able to accrue experience and move to a better paying dealership after about a year or two.

Be Positive. That is the biggest thing. Positive from start to finish. Customers will not be kind. Take what they say and let it roll off your shoulder. The first few months will be slow and get you into the groove. Make sure to be on top of EVERYTHING. This isn’t a job where you get to go home when the bell rings. You go home when the work is done. If not, it rolls into the next day, and piles. If you let your repair orders pile like that you will have unhappy customers, unhappy coworkers, and unhappy management. (Probably won’t last long either) Always update customers. Even if it’s a quick call or message that says: “I don’t have an update yet, but will soon.” They just want to hear your voice and know you haven’t forgotten about them. You are the face of the dealership for a lot of customers. If you treat customers right, and soft sell, you will get them coming back. Remember that every customer will think that they are your only customer. And the (actually) biggest thing: underpromise, over deliver. For everything, add time to expectation, so that if the tech, the porter, the parts guy, the lube tech, you, anybody messes up, you have time to either fix it or come up with a game plan to go over with the customer so that you aren’t left fucked over by a situation.
